newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan nuclear firm admits 11 past radiation leaks.
newsitem.headline: Japan nuclear firm admits 11 past radiation leaks.

text.p: The state-run Japanese firm responsible for a series of cover-ups over nuclear accidents said there had been 11 unreported radiation leaks since late 1994 at the plant where the latest mishap occurred.

Radioactive tritium leaked from the Fugen reactor in western Japan 11 times between November 1994 and January 1997, officials of the Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC) said late on Wednesday.
On Tuesday, the PNC was ordered to halt Fugen after the PNC said it waited 30 hours before reporting a leak on Monday which exposed 11 workers to small doses of radiation.
Fugen, located in Fukui Prefecture on the Sea of Japan coast about 350 km (220 miles) west of Tokyo, is an advanced thermal reactor that runs on heavy water.
In response to controversy over this week's delayed report, a senior PNC official on Wednesday night admitted there had been 11 previously unreported radiation leaks at Fugen since November 1994.
"A high density of tritium has been released outside the reactor 11 times (since November 1994)," Toshiaki Kawamura, deputy head of the Fugen facility, told a news conference.

Kawamura said his office did not report these accidents because the amounts of radioactive material released were below levels at which they would have been legally required to submit reports to the authorities.
"The leakages were far below the legally set minimum danger level, but we will report to authorities in the future as soon as a warning is issued," Kawamura said.
But Fukui prefectural officials said some of these accidents should have been reported and suspected another cover-up.

"Some of the past 11 cases did set off automatic alarms, and at least these accidents should have been reported," a spokesman for Fukui Prefecture said. "We suspect the PNC does not fully understand the agreement (on mandatory reports)."

The agreement between PNC and local governments says the power firm must report all "serious" accidents, meaning all accidents which set off automatic alarms. Kawamura said two of the past 11 accidents did set off these alarms.
On Wednesday, the Science and Technology Agency, which oversees Japan's nuclear power programme, filed a criminal complaint with police against the PNC and several company officials.

The complaint, which would initiate legal action against the PNC or its officials, concerns a falsified report on a March 11 fire and explosion at a reprocessing plant north of Tokyo, which exposed 37 workers to low levels of radiation.
Following up on the complaint, police in Ibaraki Prefecture, north of Tokyo, where the reprocessing plant is located, on Thursday began questioning PNC officials.
In another incident in late 1995, the PNC admitted lying about inspections and suppressing videotape footage of a coolant leak at its Monju experimental fast-breeder reactor.
